comparisons.evidence: P proposes an "Open-access/same-day scheduling model" to shrink the decay window. Q introduces "Automatic modality failover" and "Condition-triggered follow-up," reframing the objective around "clinically useful encounters completed." Q targets the absolute optimization of the clinician's fixed time, addressing a more systemic bottleneck than P's adjustment of booking windows.

P offers logical hypotheses for its interventions, such as "Co-presence + light social contract raises attendance" for group slots. Q anchors its primary mechanisms in empirical reality, explicitly integrating published medical literature (PubMed citations) to validate the causal pathways of its failover and condition-triggered models.

P's wildcard "Patient-to-patient appointment resale/trade board" introduces severe clinical sorting, privacy, and equity hurdles in a public chain context. Q manages operational constraints gracefully, building guardrails directly into the design of its top idea, such as checking for clinical eligibility at booking and waiting a strict "five minutes after the scheduled time" before executing a fallback.

While P outlines clean testing structures ("Convert 20% of one primary-care clinic's slots..."), Q provides exceptional testing specifications. Q outlines exact parameters for tracking success (e.g., "clinician minutes, unresolved cases, and results by age, language") alongside explicit financial and operational kill metrics.

P uses creative concepts like the "resale/trade board," but Q demonstrates a structural leap in creativity. By mapping atomic principles from cloud computing ("Modality failover," "Chain-wide care window") and industrial maintenance ("Condition-triggered follow-up"), Q completely transforms the problem from a patient-compliance issue into a resource-architecture design challenge.

P spans a highly diverse solution space covering social mechanics ("Peer accountability network"), spatial delivery ("Satellite mini-clinics"), and scheduling operations. Q matches this diversity through a structurally rich mix of network pooling ("Chain-wide care window"), administrative shifts ("Employer protected-time handshake"), and clinical workflow modularity.

P curates the reader's focus efficiently, evaluating a tight list of 11 distinct options down to 9 well-mapped survivors. Q delivers excellent analysis but dilutes its initial pool with 16 candidates, introducing near-duplicates and adjacent concepts (like "Rolling-entry group clinic" and "Certainty-class booking") that create unnecessary volume.
